newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran conservatives send Khatami warning signs.
newsitem.headline: Iran conservatives send Khatami warning signs.

text.p: Iran's influential conservatives are sending new President Mohammad Khatami warning signals ahead of expected friction over cabinet ministers.

Khatami, sworn in on Monday as Iran's fifth president since the 1979 Islamic revolution, has yet to present the conservative-dominated parliament his cabinet list for approval. By law he has to do so by August 18. Analysts and newspapers predict some controversial figures will be on the list.

"Persons who in the past have not moved in the direction of people's needs will not obtain (a) positive vote in the Majlis (parliament)," conservative MP Marzieh Sadighi was quoted as saying by the evening daily Resalat on Monday.

"Failure by a number of ministers to obtain a vote of confidence from the Majlis should not be considered as a confrontation with the president," she told the newspaper, which is close to conservative powers.

Analysts see Khatami's success in passing his cabinet list through the 270-member parliament as the first test of strength in future battles if, backed by 20 million voters, he embarks on a programme to deliver promised social justice and relax the clergy-led system of rule.
Khatami himself was forced to resign as culture minister in 1992 under conservative pressure for what they saw as his failure to combat a Western cultural invasion.
The new head of the executive has yet to officially announce his ministers but hardline newspapers have already started attacking likely candidates.

Among the targets is Ataollah Mohajerani who several newspapers said would take over the ministry of culture and Islamic guidance. Mohajerani came under severe attack in the late 1980s for proposing in an article the holding of direct talks with Iran's declared enemy the United States.

The culture ministry "is in fact the command headquarters against the enemy's cultural invasion and therefore it should not be taken over by cowards or those who do not hold a grudge against America in their hearts," the hardline Jomhouri Eslami said in an editorial.
It did not name Mohajerani but said this "includes those who had proposed direct talks with America".
The same daily had published several attacks against Khatami's apparent choice for foreign minister -- United Nations envoy Kamal Kharrazi.
"Iran needs a revolutionary foreign minister who can give our foreign policy new mobility and consistency," it said on Monday.

Kharrazi, who has a U.S. doctorate in management psychology, told Reuters on Monday he had been approached to head the foreign ministry -- replacing Ali Akbar Velayati who has held the post since two years after the revolution.
"There have been discussions with me," he said. When asked if he had accepted, Kharrazi said: "But we have to wait until the cabinet is presented to parliament."
On Monday Khatami told parliament "We think that dialogue between civilisations is essential in today's world. We will avoid any action or behaviour leading to (world) tension."

Parliament speaker, Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, and the head of the judiciary, Ayatollah Mohammad Yazdi, both indirectly hinted in speeches on Monday that Khatami should consult parliament ahead of presenting a cabinet list. Other conservatives are also dissatisfied with his failure to do so.
Khatami in May defeated Nateq-Nouri, who had been tipped to win the elections but only secured about seven million out of 29.1 million votes.
